summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell activation syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and single-vessel coronary artery disease was admitted for progressive chest pain lasting four days, atypical for ischemia. She denied a mast cell flare but requested her usual IV medications. Evaluation showed no myocardial necrosis on serial troponins, unchanged EKG, and a retrocardiac opacity on chest X-ray likely due to atelectasis. Her cardiac catheterization from an outside hospital revealed a 90% ostial stenosis in a diagonal branch of the LAD and a 70% mid-LAD lesion, but no urgent revascularization was indicated. She was continued on medical therapy for CAD, including aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, and nitrate, with cardiology follow-up planned to discuss CABG. Mast cell regimen was maintained with oral antihistamines and a one-time IV Benadryl. She improved symptomatically and was discharged home with stable vital signs and a plan for outpatient follow-up with cardiology and pulmonology.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
